# The Off-Ramp: The 90-Day Plan for Keeping Your Results After GLP-1s
> The shot did the heavy lifting. This is the plan for everything after.
*Ramp down, not crash down.*

## Before You Start
If you are holding this, one of three things probably just happened. Your prescriber said it is time to come down. Your insurance stopped paying, or the price stopped making sense. Or you decided you want to find out who you are without a weekly injection. Whichever it was, you are likely carrying the same worry almost everyone carries at this point: *what if it all comes back?*
Put the shame down first, because you will need both hands. Studies keep finding that roughly half of people who start a GLP-1 for weight stop within a year. You are not the exception. You are the majority. And when people stop, appetite usually returns, because the medicine was doing a job your biology will now try to undo. That is physiology, not a verdict on your willpower.
Here is what is also true: almost nobody is handed a plan for this part. You got a schedule for going *up*. You got a leaflet about nausea. For the way down you got one appointment, a shrug, or nothing. Clinicians themselves say there is no standard protocol yet for life after the medication.
This workbook is that missing plan. It will not tell you how to taper; that is your prescriber's call, and Part 1 helps you have that conversation well. It gives you what the medication cannot: a protein floor, a strength minimum, a way to handle food noise when it comes back, and a decision, made in advance, about what you will do if the scale climbs.
Ninety days. One page a week. A set of cards for the hard moments in between.
The promise is not that nothing will change. Something will. The promise is that when it does, you will already know what to do, and you will be doing it from a plan instead of a panic.
*Ramp down, not crash down.*

## Why This Works
### What the medication was doing
GLP-1 medicines such as semaglutide (Wegovy, Ozempic) and tirzepatide (Zepbound, Mounjaro) imitate gut hormones that tell your brain you have eaten enough. They slow how fast your stomach empties, and for many people they turn down the constant background chatter about food that people call **food noise**. When you stop, those effects fade over a few weeks as the drug clears your system. The timing depends on the drug and the dose.
### What usually happens next
In the STEP 1 trial extension, people who stopped semaglutide regained about two-thirds of the weight they had lost within a year. In SURMOUNT-4, people switched from tirzepatide to a placebo regained more than half of what they had lost, even with continued diet and activity counseling. Those are averages. They tell you the pull is real and strong. They do not tell you your number, and some people in both trials kept much of their loss.
### The three levers this book pulls
**1. Protect the muscle.** Some of the weight lost on GLP-1s is lean mass. Resistance training and enough protein are the best-supported ways to protect and rebuild it. Muscle matters for strength, for blood sugar handling and for aging well.
**2. Build structure before the appetite returns.** Anchored meals, a quieter kitchen and responses decided in advance mean fewer decisions get made while you are hungry. Research on people who keep weight off long term keeps finding the same habits: consistent eating patterns, plenty of daily movement and regular self-monitoring.
**3. Catch small changes early.** A few pounds noticed and acted on is a very different problem from twenty pounds discovered in March. That is what your Tripwire Plan is for.

## What This Book Is Not
**It is not medical advice.** Nothing here tells you whether, when or how to stop, taper or restart a medication. That is a decision for you and your prescriber, and Part 1 exists so you walk into that appointment with the right questions.
**It is not a taper schedule.** You will find no doses in this book, on purpose.
**It is not a diet.** There are no calorie targets and no banned foods. There is a protein floor, which is a minimum, not a maximum, and a set of habits.
**It is not a substitute for your care team.** If you have type 2 diabetes, stopping a GLP-1 can change your blood sugar, and that needs monitoring agreed with your clinician. If you take blood pressure or diabetes medicines, ask whether anything needs adjusting when you stop.
**It is not right for everyone as written.** If you have a history of disordered eating, weighing, tracking and rules can do harm. See "Make It Fit Your Life" before you begin.
What it is: the plan nobody handed you, built from the parts of the evidence that are solid, written so you can actually use it on a Tuesday night.

## Your Day 1 Scores
Fill this in today, before Week 1. On Day 90 you will score the same things again, side by side. Feelings are slippery; numbers you wrote yourself are not.
- Food noise (0 = silent, 10 = constant)
- Confidence I can keep my results (0 to 10)
- Energy on a normal afternoon (0 to 10)
- 30-second chair stands (Count, see the note below)
- Days I hit my protein floor (Out of the last 7)
- Waist at the belly button (optional) (Inches or cm)
**The chair-stand test:** sit in a sturdy chair without arms, feet flat, arms crossed over your chest. Count how many times you can stand fully and sit back down in 30 seconds. It is a simple strength check used by clinicians. Skip it if it is not safe for you.

## What to Expect
Most plans fail at a predictable moment, and the moment is predictable because it is chemical. Here is the usual shape of the next ninety days, so nothing surprises you.
**Weeks 1 to 2, The Coast.** The medication is still partly in your system. Appetite stays low and you may wonder what the fuss was about. This is your best window: build the floors now, while it is easy. The risk here is complacency.
**Weeks 3 to 6, The Return.** Appetite and food noise come back, sometimes gradually, sometimes all at once. Portions creep. The scale may jump a few pounds from water and the simple fact that there is more food in you. This is the wobble, and it is planned for: the cards in Part 3 exist for exactly these weeks.
**Weeks 7 to 9, The Test.** The novelty is gone, the noise is back and the plan starts to feel like work. This is where most plans quietly die. It is also why there is a letter waiting for you at the halfway point.
**Weeks 10 to 12, The Settle.** The routines start running without you pushing them. You know your noise patterns, you know your numbers, and you have three months of evidence about what works for you.
Somewhere around Week 4 you will probably want to quit. That is not a sign the plan is failing. It is a sign it is Week 4.

## The Rule for Bad Days: The No-Catch-Up Rule
You will miss things. Everyone does. What decides how the next ninety days go is not whether you miss, it is what you do next. So here is the rule, and it has no exceptions:
- **No catching up.** Missed a strength session? You do not do two next time. You do the next one.
- **No compensating.** Ate the whole thing? The next meal is a normal meal at your protein floor. Not a skipped meal, not a punishment salad.
- **No restarts.** You never go back to Week 1. You do not "start again on Monday." You do today.
One off day is information. Three off days in a row is a signal, and the signal has a card: open Card 10, "I haven't done any of this for a week."
*The tick-grid is a record, not a courtroom.*

## Make It Fit Your Life
**You lost access suddenly, with no taper.** You are starting Week 1 with less runway, because the medication may wear off faster than it would on a planned step-down. Do the 7-Day Quickstart (in the bonus pages) first, then begin Week 1. Still book the prescriber conversation, even if more medication is off the table: you need the follow-up for blood pressure, blood work and a plan.
**You have type 2 diabetes.** Stopping a GLP-1 can raise blood sugar. Agree a monitoring plan with your care team before you stop, and add a glucose row to your weekly page if they ask you to track it. Their numbers outrank anything in this book.
**You work shifts or keep odd hours.** "Breakfast, lunch and dinner" means your first, middle and last meal after waking, whatever the clock says. The floors and the rules work the same way.
**You have joint pain, an injury or limited mobility.** The Minimum Strength Session has seated and supported versions. If anything hurts in a sharp way, stop, and ask your clinician about a referral to a physical therapist. It is one of the most useful referrals you can ask for.
**You have a history of disordered eating.** Skip all weighing and do not track numbers. Use this book only alongside a professional who knows your history. Reaching out is the strong move here, not the weak one: the ANAD helpline is listed in the small print at the back.

## Part 1: Before the Ramp
Three pages and about an hour. These are the decisions you would rather not make while you are hungry, so you make them now, while you are calm.

### The Prescriber Conversation
Bring this page to your appointment, or a phone photo of it. Write the answers in while you are in the room. If time runs short, ask questions 1, 4 and 6 first.
1. Should I stop all at once, step down gradually, or stay on a lower dose for maintenance? Why that option for me?
2. If we step down, what is the schedule, and what should make me call you before the next step?
3. Which checks do you want, and when? (Blood pressure, blood sugar or A1c, cholesterol, anything else.)
4. How much weight regain should make me call you? Can we set a number together?
5. If I want to restart later, what would that look like? Would I start again at the lowest dose?
6. Do any of my other medications need adjusting when I stop?
7. Can you refer me to a registered dietitian or a physical therapist? Is it covered?

### Your Floors
A floor is the minimum you do on your worst week. Not your goal, not your ideal: the floor. Good weeks will go above it on their own.
**Floor 1: Protein.** Many clinicians and dietitians suggest somewhere around 1.2 to 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day during and after weight loss. Some people need more, and some need less, including many people with kidney disease. Ask your clinician or dietitian for your number, then do the arithmetic below.
- My weight in pounds ÷ 2.2 = kilograms
- Kilograms × my target (for example 1.2) = grams per day
- Grams per day ÷ number of meals = my per-meal floor
Most people land somewhere around 25 to 40 grams per meal. The Protein Floor Cheat Sheet in the bonus pages shows what that looks like on a plate.
**Floor 2: Strength.** Two sessions a week of the 20-Minute Minimum Session (bonus pages), or your own equivalent. My two days are:
**Floor 3: Daily movement.** Check your phone or watch for your average daily steps over the last week, then add 1,000. Not walking much right now? Start from where you are; any number above today counts.

### Your Tripwire Plan
You decide now, while calm, exactly what you will do if the numbers move. Then, if they do, you are following a plan rather than having a feeling about it.
- **Green:** Within ____ of my stop weight. Keep doing the weekly page. Nothing else changes.
- **Yellow:** Between ____ and ____ above my stop weight. For two weeks: hit my protein floor at every meal, log food noise every day, do both strength sessions, and read Card 7.
- **Red:** More than ____ above, or food noise at 8+ most days for two weeks. Call my prescriber (the number we set in question 4) and book a dietitian. Read Part 4, The Restart Question.
If your prescriber did not give you numbers, a common starting point is a Yellow line at about 3% above your stop weight and a Red line at about 5%. Researchers often treat a change under 3% as "maintained" and a change of 5% or more as meaningful. Not weighing? Use your waist measurement or one honest pair of jeans instead.

## Part 2: The Twelve Weeks
One page a week, the same shape every time, so your thumb always knows where to go. Read the page on Sunday. Tick the grid each evening. Write one honest line at the end of the week.

### Week 1 (The Coast): The Floor Rule
**Every meal starts with protein, and the protein gets to your floor before anything else does.**
Right now the medication is still partly working, so your appetite is low. That makes this the easiest week of the ninety to build the habit that matters most.
For most people protein is the most filling thing on the plate, and it is the raw material for the muscle you want to keep. Many people coming off a GLP-1 discover they ate very little protein for months, simply because they barely ate.
This week's move:
- Choose three breakfasts, three lunches and three dinners that reach your per-meal floor. Write them on the Protein Floor Cheat Sheet.
- At every meal, eat the protein part first.
- Shop for those nine meals this week, so the floor is the easy option.
Tracked daily: protein floor, Protein eaten first, food noise peak.

### Week 2 (The Coast): The Lift Rule
**Twice a week, you lift something heavy enough to notice.**
Some of the weight lost on GLP-1s is lean mass, and muscle does not come back on its own. Resistance training is the best-supported way to protect and rebuild it.
You do not need a gym, a trainer or an outfit. You need twenty minutes, a sturdy chair, a wall and something with a handle. Heavy enough to notice means the last two repetitions feel like work.
This week's move:
- Put two 20-minute sessions in your calendar like appointments.
- Do the 20-Minute Minimum Session from the bonus pages.
- Redo your chair-stand count at the end of the week and write it below.
Tracked daily: protein floor, Strength session, food noise peak.

### Week 3 (The Return): The Name-It Rule
**When food noise shows up, name it, score it and give it ten minutes.**
For many people this is the week the noise starts coming back. Cravings tend to rise, peak and fall like a wave rather than building forever. Psychologists call riding one out without fighting or obeying it "urge surfing," and it has research support for cravings of many kinds.
Naming the thought puts a little space between you and it. "I want cookies" is an order. "That is food noise, about a 6" is a weather report.
This week's move:
- When a food thought arrives outside a planned meal, say "that is noise" and score it from 0 to 10.
- Set a 10-minute timer and give your hands something to do.
- When it rings, decide on purpose. Sometimes the answer is yes, and that is fine.
Tracked daily: protein floor, Noise named + 10 min, food noise peak.

### Week 4 (The Return): The Plate Order Rule
**Protein and vegetables first. Starch last.**
Some small studies have found that eating vegetables and protein before carbohydrates leads to smaller blood sugar spikes after a meal, and many people find it fills them up sooner. It is not magic. It is sequencing.
The medication slowed your stomach down. Now you slow your fork down instead. Fullness signals take time to arrive, and a meal eaten in eight minutes outruns them.
This week's move:
- At every meal: protein and vegetables first, starch and sweet things last.
- At dinner, put your fork down between bites.
- Aim for one meal a day that takes 20 minutes.
Tracked daily: protein floor, Plate order kept, food noise peak.

### Week 5 (The Return): The Pantry Rule
**If it is in your line of sight, it is in your diet.**
Food noise is louder when food is visible. Research on food environments keeps finding that people eat more of whatever is in sight and within easy reach, regardless of intentions.
You cannot out-willpower your own kitchen every evening for the rest of your life. You can rearrange it once.
This week's move:
- Do a 15-minute kitchen reset: your loudest foods go out of sight or out of the house.
- Put protein options and fruit at eye level in the fridge.
- Buy treats in single portions, so "having some" has an ending.
Tracked daily: protein floor, Kitchen closed after dinner, food noise peak.

### Week 6 (The Return): The Weekly Average Rule
**You read the weekly average, never the single morning.**
Your weight swings from day to day with water, salt, hormones and how much food is in your system. In the weeks after stopping, simply eating more volume can add a few pounds of water and food weight. A single morning number causes panic; a seven-day average shows the trend.
People who keep weight off long term commonly check in on it regularly. The point is calm information, not judgment.
This week's move:
- If weighing is healthy for you, weigh under the same conditions each morning.
- On Sunday, average the week and compare it with your Tripwire zones.
- Not weighing? Measure your waist once a week instead.
Tracked daily: protein floor, Weighed, no reaction, food noise peak.

### Halfway
You are six weeks in. The medication is most likely out of your system by now, the noise has had time to come back, and the plan has stopped being new.
Here is the honest part: this exact spot, weeks six to eight, is where most attempts like this quietly end. Not with a decision, but with a skipped Sunday page that turns into two. Nobody ever decides to stop. They just stop opening the book.
So, three things before you turn the page.
**Look at your grids.** Not at what you missed, at what you did. Count the ticks. That number is real, and it is yours.
**Check your zone.** Green? Good, carry on. Yellow? Your plan already says what to do, and doing it is not failing, it is the plan working. Red? Make the call. That is the strong move.
**Lower the bar if you need to.** On a bad week, the floors are enough. Protein first, two short sessions, and the cards when it gets loud. That is still the plan.
*This exact moment is the whole game.*

### Week 7 (The Test): The Hungry or Noisy Rule
**Before you eat off-plan, ask three questions.**
**1. When did I last eat a floor meal?** If it was more than four or five hours ago, you may simply be hungry. Hungry gets fed, properly, with a real meal.
**2. Would I eat an apple or plain chicken right now?** If yes, it is probably hunger. If only one specific food will do, it is probably noise.
**3. What happened in the last 30 minutes?** Stress, boredom, an argument, an ad: that is noise. Noise gets the ten minutes from Week 3.
This week's move:
- Ask the three questions every time you reach for food off-plan.
- Keep a tally this week: how many hungry, how many noisy.
Tracked daily: protein floor, Three questions asked, food noise peak.

### Week 8 (The Test): The Liquid Rule
**Drinks are decided before you are holding one.**
Many people drank less alcohol on GLP-1s, and some research suggests these drugs can reduce the desire to drink. When that desire comes back, alcohol adds energy of its own and lowers the guardrails on food at the same time.
Sugary coffees, juices and sodas count too. Liquid calories tend to fill you up less than the same calories eaten as food.
This week's move:
- On Sunday, write your drink plan for the week: the maximum number of alcoholic drinks, and when.
- Alternate every alcoholic drink with a glass of water.
- Sweet drinks are planned, not reached for.
Tracked daily: protein floor, Drink plan kept, food noise peak.

### Week 9 (The Test): The Sleep Rule
**Protect seven hours as if it were prescribed.**
Research keeps finding that short sleep is linked with more hunger and more eating. In laboratory studies, people who were short of sleep ate noticeably more the next day.
A tired brain goes looking for quick energy, and the noise is always louder at 11pm than at 9am. Some of your evening cravings are really a bedtime problem.
This week's move:
- Keep the same wake-up time all seven days, weekends included.
- Screens down 30 minutes before bed.
- The kitchen closes after dinner; that rule from Week 5 earns its keep this week.
Tracked daily: protein floor, 7 hours in bed, food noise peak.

### Week 10 (The Settle): The Social Plate Rule
**Decide before you arrive.**
Restaurants, holidays and family dinners bring big portions, other people's expectations and usually a drink or two, all at the moment your plan is easiest to drop.
The fix is not avoiding people. It is making the decision at home, where nobody is passing you anything.
This week's move:
- Before a meal out, look at the menu and choose your protein.
- Eat a small protein snack before you leave.
- Choose one "worth it" item on purpose, and enjoy every bite of it. Use the scripts in the bonus pages for the people who push.
Tracked daily: protein floor, Plan made before going, food noise peak.

### Week 11 (The Settle): The Steps Rule
**Move a little all day, not a lot once.**
The movement you do outside of workouts, such as walking, standing and chores, is a large and underrated share of the energy you use each day. People who keep weight off long term commonly report high levels of everyday activity, much of it walking.
Some studies also suggest a short walk after a meal helps blunt the rise in blood sugar that follows it.
This week's move:
- Hit your step floor from Part 1 each day.
- Take a 10-minute walk after your biggest meal.
- Stand up for one phone call a day.
Tracked daily: protein floor, Walk after biggest meal, food noise peak.

### Week 12 (The Settle): The Keep Rule
**Keep what worked. Drop what did not. Write it down.**
The point was never ninety days of effort. The point is a routine you would happily keep for a year. Look back at your eleven grids: some rules happened almost without effort, and some you fought every week.
The easy ones are your keepers. The ones you fought are either not for you, or not for you yet. Both answers are useful.
This week's move:
- Read back through your weekly pages and circle the rules that stuck.
- Fill in the Keep Five card at the end of the book.
- Put a monthly check-in in your calendar, and book a follow-up with your prescriber.
Tracked daily: protein floor, Keepers chosen, food noise peak.

## Part 3: The Food Noise Cards
For the moments that do not wait until Sunday. Find the card that matches how you feel right now, do what it says, then note it in the Card Log at the back.

### Card 1: It is late and I am standing at the pantry.
What is happening: Evening is when willpower is lowest and noise is loudest, especially if you are tired.
Say this: "This is the 9pm noise. It always comes and it always goes."
1. Close the door and move to another room.
2. Brush your teeth. It is a strong "eating is over" signal.
3. If you are truly hungry, have a planned protein snack, sitting down, on a plate.

### Card 2: I ate far more than I planned and today feels ruined.
What is happening: One big meal does very little to your trend. What does the damage is the "might as well" that comes after it.
Say this: "One meal is one meal. The next one is normal."
1. No skipping and no punishing. The next meal is a normal floor meal.
2. Take a 10-minute walk if you can.
3. Tick what you did do today. There was something.

### Card 3: The scale jumped overnight.
What is happening: Water, salt, hormones and digestion can move the scale a few pounds in a day. Fat does not appear overnight.
Say this: "That is weather. I read the weekly average."
1. Write the number down and do not react to it.
2. Drink water and eat your floor meals as normal.
3. Wait for Sunday's average before deciding anything.

### Card 4: I am stressed, bored or sad, and food is the plan.
What is happening: Food is a fast, reliable comfort. The feeling is real; it just is not hunger.
Say this: "I am not hungry. I am stressed (or bored, or sad), and I can help that."
1. Name the actual feeling out loud.
2. Pick one non-food reset: a walk, a shower, a call, five minutes outside.
3. After that, if you still want it, have a portion on purpose.

### Card 5: The food noise is back and it is loud all day.
What is happening: This is the Return. It usually peaks in weeks three to six and settles as routines take over.
Say this: "Loud does not mean in charge."
1. Go back to basics: protein first at every meal, no grazing in between.
2. Score the noise each day this week so you can see whether it is falling.
3. If it is 8 or higher most days for two weeks, that is a Red-zone item: call your prescriber.

### Card 6: I am at a party or a buffet and everything is right there.
What is happening: Variety and visibility both increase how much people eat. Buffets combine both.
Say this: "I will have the best thing here, not everything here."
1. Walk the whole table once before you take a plate.
2. Protein and vegetables first, then one "worth it" item.
3. Stand or sit facing away from the food.

### Card 7: I hit my Yellow zone.
What is happening: This is the Tripwire working exactly as designed: you caught it early.
Say this: "Yellow is a plan, not a verdict."
1. Open your Tripwire page and follow the Yellow actions for two weeks.
2. Log food noise every day.
3. Re-check the weekly average in two Sundays. Most Yellows turn Green with the basics.

### Card 8: I am thinking about restarting and I feel like I failed.
What is happening: Wanting to restart is common. In one large 2026 analysis, more than half of people with type 2 diabetes who stopped a GLP-1 restarted within a year.
Say this: "This is a medical decision, not a moral one."
1. Read Part 4, The Restart Question.
2. Fill in its checklist honestly.
3. Book the appointment. Asking the question is not the same as deciding.

### Card 9: I cannot afford it anymore, or my coverage stopped.
What is happening: Losing access is one of the most common reasons people stop. It is a money problem, not a personal failure.
Say this: "The medication stopped. The plan did not."
1. Ask your insurer which criteria changed, and whether an appeal or prior authorization is possible.
2. Ask your prescriber about lower-cost options and what follow-up you still need.
3. Do the 7-Day Quickstart if you had no taper.

### Card 10: I have not done any of this for a week.
What is happening: Gaps happen to everyone. The plan only fails if the gap becomes the new plan.
Say this: "No catching up. Just today."
1. Do not restart at Week 1. Open the page for the week you are actually in.
2. Do just the floors today: protein first and one short walk.
3. Write one line in "What I noticed" about why the gap happened.

## Part 4: The Restart Question
*Restarting is a medical decision, not a moral one.*
Many clinicians now treat obesity as a long-term condition, and compare GLP-1s to blood pressure or cholesterol medicines, which nobody expects you to "graduate" from. Some people keep their results without medication. Some do not. Both are outcomes of biology, not character.
If you are wondering whether to restart, you do not have to decide alone or decide today. Use this page to get your thoughts in order, and bring it to your prescriber.
**Signs it is worth a conversation (tick any that apply)**
- [ ] I am in my Red zone, or I have been in Yellow for more than four weeks despite the Yellow actions.
- [ ] Food noise has been 8 or higher on most days for two weeks or more.
- [ ] My blood sugar, blood pressure or other checks are moving in the wrong direction.
- [ ] It is affecting my mood, sleep or how I feel about myself.
**Questions to bring**
- Would a lower maintenance dose be an option for me, rather than my old full dose?
- Would I need to start again at the lowest dose?
- What would this cost me, and does my plan have new requirements to restart?
- If I restart, how should my Off-Ramp plan change?
Whatever you decide, the floors stay. Protein, strength and steps help whether you are on medication or off it.

## Your Day 90 Scores
Copy your Day 1 numbers into the first column, then score yourself today. Same measures, same honesty.
Whatever the numbers say, they are yours, measured by you, over ninety days. That is evidence, not enthusiasm.

## The Keep Five
Choose the five habits from the last twelve weeks that you will keep for the next twelve months. Choose the ones that felt almost easy. Write them here, then copy them onto a card for the fridge.
- My monthly check-in day:
- My Yellow line:
- My Red line:
- My prescriber's number:
- My next appointment:
The ramp is behind you. The road is yours now.

## Bonus 1: The 7-Day Quickstart
For anyone who stopped suddenly, or is stopping this week and has no time to read. One job a day. Then start Week 1.
- **Day 1:** Score your Day 1 page. Ten minutes, no more.
- **Day 2:** Work out your protein floor and write down three meals that reach it.
- **Day 3:** Do your first 20-Minute Minimum Session.
- **Day 4:** Do the 15-minute kitchen reset from Week 5.
- **Day 5:** Book the prescriber appointment and fill in your Tripwire numbers as far as you can.
- **Day 6:** Read the Food Noise Cards once, all the way through, so you know where they are.
- **Day 7:** Second strength session, then read the Week 1 page. You are ready.

## Bonus 3: The 20-Minute Minimum Session
No gym required. Warm up for three minutes (march on the spot, roll your shoulders), then do two or three rounds of the five moves below, resting as long as you need between them.
- **Sit-to-stand** (8 to 12): Stand up from a sturdy chair and sit back down with control. Easier: use your hands. Harder: hold a weight at your chest.
- **Wall or counter push-up** (8 to 12): Hands on a wall or kitchen counter, body straight, lower your chest and push away. Harder: use a lower surface.
- **Glute bridge** (10 to 12): Lie on your back with knees bent and lift your hips. Seated version: squeeze and hold for five seconds.
- **One-arm row** (10 each side): Lean on a counter and pull a gallon jug, a loaded backpack or a dumbbell toward your ribs.
- **Carry** (30 to 40 sec): Walk holding two heavy grocery bags, shoulders back. Supported version: hold them standing still.
**The progression rule:** when you can do the top number of repetitions with good form in every round, make it a little harder: a lower surface, a heavier jug or a slower pace on the way down.
If you have a heart condition, high blood pressure that is not controlled, or a joint problem, check with your clinician first. Stop any movement that causes sharp pain.

## Bonus 4: What to Say When
The cards handle the noise inside your head. These handle the people outside it. Say them word for word, or make them your own.
- **"Were you on Ozempic?"** "I was, with my doctor. Now I'm working on the part nobody talks about: keeping it." Or simply: "That's between me and my doctor."
- **"You're off the shot, so you can have dessert now!"** "I can, and I'll pick when. Not tonight, but thank you."
- **"Have seconds, I made it for you."** "It's so good I want it again tomorrow. Could I take some home?"
- **"Just one drink."** "I'm set with this one," while holding the one you planned.
- **To your partner or housemate** "Here's how you can help this month: keep the snacks in your cupboard, not the shared one, invite me on walks, and please don't comment on my plate."
- **To a rushed prescriber** "Before we finish, I need a plan for what to do if my weight goes up after stopping. Can we set a number together?"
- **To your insurer or pharmacy** "Can you tell me exactly which coverage criteria changed, and whether an appeal or a prior authorization is possible?"

## The Honest Small Print
This workbook is general education about habits and routines. It is not medical advice, and it does not replace your prescriber, a registered dietitian, a physical therapist or a mental health professional. Never stop, change or restart a medication because of anything in this book; make those decisions with your clinician.
Results vary. The research described here reports averages from groups of people, and your experience may be better or worse than those averages. Nothing in this book is a promise of a particular weight or outcome.
Wegovy, Ozempic, Zepbound and Mounjaro are trademarks of their respective owners. This workbook is independent and is not affiliated with or endorsed by any drug manufacturer.
- **ANAD eating disorder helpline:** 1-888-375-7767 (anad.org)
- **988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline:** Call or text 988 (US)
- **Find a registered dietitian:** eatright.org, "Find a Nutrition Expert"
- **Emergency:** Call 911 or your local emergency number
Be as patient with yourself as you would be with a friend doing this. Ramp down, not crash down.
